# Saving Limbs, Changing Lives:

## Synchrotron Radiation Clinical Trial for dogs with Soft Tissue Sarcoma

This groundbreaking trial is the first of its kind, offering an alternative treatment for dogs with distal limb soft tissue sarcomas that would otherwise require amputation. By utilising advanced Synchrotron radiation therapy, this study aims to provide a potentially curative, limb-sparing option, offering new hope for dogs facing this challenging diagnosis.

##### Advancing Cancer Treatment in Dogs: Synchrotron Radiation Therapy Pilot Study

Dr. Arthur House and Dr. Eleanor Woolley have been collaborating for the past four years with nuclear physicists and medical radiation therapists from Australia’s Nuclear Science and Technology Organisation (ANSTO) at the Australian Synchrotron. Their work has led to the establishment of a pilot study assessing the efficacy of Synchrotron radiation therapy in managing canine soft tissue sarcoma.

Soft tissue sarcomas, particularly when large, can become unresectable, often requiring limb amputation to achieve oncologic control. This study aims to evaluate whether Synchrotron radiation can provide a curative alternative for these challenging cases.

Why Synchrotron Radiation?
Unlike conventional linear accelerator radiation, Synchrotron radiation offers several advantages:
✔ Single-visit treatment – Delivers a full course of radiation in just one session.
✔ Enhanced normal tissue tolerance – Potentially reducing side effects compared to standard radiotherapy.

Enrolment Opportunity for Canine Patients
We have the opportunity to enrol 12 dogs with distal limb soft tissue sarcomas in this pilot study. Eligible patients will receive Synchrotron radiation therapy with the goal of curative intent, providing a novel treatment pathway for cases where surgery may not be viable.

##### Clinical trial details

Prior to enrolment the dogs will have tumour staging performed, including serum biochemistry, haematology, histopathology and CT imaging for metastases check and treatment planning at Peninsula Vet Emergency & Referral Hospital.

Once enrolled, the patient will have a single radiation treatment at the Australian Synchrotron under the care of our vet, nurse and anaesthetist team. Follow-up checks will be performed weekly, monitoring the tumour shrinkage, until the time of tumour resection 4-6 weeks post treatment.

##### Eligibility

For dogs to be eligible for the trial they must be suitable for general anaesthesia, free of known systemic or metastatic disease, and have a distal limb (below the elbow or below the stifle) soft tissue sarcoma, prior to surgery.

# Unleashing the Potential of Microbeam Radiation Therapy in Spontaneous Canine Sarcoma Treatment

---

**Introduction:** Microbeam Radiation Therapy (MRT) is a form of submillimetre spatially fractionated radiotherapy that can be delivered at the Imaging and Medical Beam Line (IMBL) of the ANSTO ANSTO. Preclinical studies demonstrate that high-dose microbeams inhibit tumour growth, disrupt tumour vasculature, and induce anti-tumour immune responses. However, the efficacy and safety of MRT must be evaluated in spontaneous cancers of similar size, growth and microenvironment to those in humans.

**Method:** Two studies investigated MRT in spontaneous canine sarcomas of the distal limb. Four dogs with osteosarcoma received a partial-field MRT to investigate in-field and out-of-field effects. Eleven dogs with soft tissue sarcoma received full-field irradiation with either MRT (n=6) or FLASH broad-beam (BB) radiotherapy (n=5). An Eclipse-hybrid planning system was used to prescribe doses to the target volumes, 5 Gy for BB and MRT valley doses (150 Gy peak). CT imaging before and after irradiation assessed tumour volumes and bone density, while MRI additionally evaluated osteosarcoma vascular permeability. Tumour tissue and serial blood and urine samples were collected for histopathological, immunological, proteomic and biochemical analyses.

**Results:** MRT reduced tumour volume in both forms of sarcoma, producing an 80% response compared to 40% with BB in soft tissue sarcomas. Despite receiving only partial irradiation, osteosarcoma regressed in 3 of 4 dogs, accompanied by increased anti-tumour immune responses and vascular disruption. CT, histology, and biochemical analyses showed that the regressing tumour was replaced by new bone via osteogenesis, supporting bone recovery. No skin toxicity or hair loss was observed at six months post-treatment. 

**Conclusion:** MRT safely and effectively treated large, spontaneous canine sarcomas, demonstrating promising anti-tumour efficacy and normal-tissue sparing.

Now Open! Clinical Trial for Dogs with Soft Tissue Sarcoma. We are thrilled to announce a groundbreaking new opportunity for pet owners and veterinarians! Peninsula Vet Emergency & Referral Hospital, in collaboration with the Australian Synchrotron and ANSTO, is now enrolling dogs in a clinical trial exploring a unique radiation therapy for appendicular soft tissue sarcomas.  Why is this exciting?  ✅ A single Synchrotron radiation treatment – more targeted, better tolerated than traditional therapies  ✅ Potentially curative radiation therapy for eligible dogs  ✅ No need for limb amputation in cases where tumours would otherwise be unresectable. Eligibility:  ✔ Dogs must be suitable for general anaesthesia  ✔ No known systemic or metastatic disease  ✔ Tumour located below the elbow or stifle. This world-first innovative trial, led by Dr. Arthur House and Dr. Eleanor Woolley, could change the future of cancer treatment for our beloved pets. If you or your clients have a dog that might qualify, we’d love to hear from you! We currently have spaces for just 12 dogs. Contact us today to learn more. https://lnkd.in/gegEzHuv

This study uses Synchrotron radiation therapy to deliver a single, targeted radiation treatment with curative intent, offering an alternative to amputation in carefully selected cases. Dogs have already undergone treatment as part of the study, with early results encouraging.
